blocks.title: Introduction
blocks.content:
[]{#sec-intro label="sec-intro"}

The story of the "volume conjecture" started with the crucial observation [@Kashaev] that the so-called Kashaev invariant of a knot $K$ defined at the $n$-th root of unity $q = e^{2 \pi i / n}$ in the classical limit has a nice asymptotic behavior determined by the hyperbolic volume $\text{Vol} (M)$ of the knot complement $M = S^3 \setminus K$. Shortly after, it was realized [@MurMur] that the Kashaev invariant is equal to the $n$-colored Jones polynomial of a knot $K$ evaluated at $q = e^{2 \pi i / n}$, so that the volume conjecture could be stated simply as

blocks.title: Generalized volume conjecture
blocks.content: Once the volume conjecture is put in the context of analytically continued Chern-Simons theory, it becomes clear that the right-hand side is simply the value of the classical $SL(2,{\mathbb C})$ Chern-Simons action functional on a knot complement $M$. Since classical solutions in Chern-Simons theory (*i.e.* flat connections on $M$) come in families, parametrized by the holonomy of the gauge connection on a small loop around the knot, this physical interpretation immediately leads to a "family version" of the volume conjecture [@Apol]: $$J_n (K; q = e^{\hbar}) \;\overset{{n \to \infty \atop \hb

blocks.title: Quantum volume conjecture
blocks.content:
Classical solutions in Chern-Simons theory (*i.e.* flat connections on $M$) are labeled by the holonomy eigenvalue $x = e^u$ or, to be more precise, by a point on the algebraic curve $${\cal C }: \quad \left\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{C}^*\times \mathbb{C}^*\Big|
A(x,y) \; = \; 0 \right\}\,,
\label{Acurve}$$ defined by the zero locus of the $A$-polynomial, a certain classical invariant of a knot. blocks.title: Quantization and deformation of algebraic curves
blocks.content:
The above structure -- and its "refinement" that we are going to construct -- is not limited to applications in knot theory. Similar mathematical structure appears in matrix models [@BIPZ; @Dijkgraaf:1990rs; @Fukuma:1990jw], in four-dimensional ${\mathcal{N}}=2$ supersymmetric gauge theories [@SW-I; @Nekrasov; @NS; @Braverman:2004cr], and in topological string theory [@ADKMV; @DHSV; @DHS; @ACDKV].

In all of these problems, the semiclassical limit is described by a certain "spectral curve" [\[Acurve\]](#Acurve){reference-type="eqref" reference="Acurve"} defined by the zero locus of $A(x,y)$. M

blocks.title: The new conjectures: incorporating $t$
blocks.content:
In this section we describe general aspects of the mathematical structure shared by a wide variety of examples, ranging from the counting of refined BPS invariants to categorification of quantum group invariants. Then, in later sections we focus on each class of examples separately.

In particular, one of our goals is to promote the volume conjectures [\[VCparam\]](#VCparam){reference-type="eqref" reference="VCparam"} and [\[VCquant\]](#VCquant){reference-type="eqref" reference="VCquant"} to the corresponding refined / categorified versions, both for knots and for the refined BPS invariants.

blocks.title: Quantum volume conjecture: refined
blocks.content: The fact that a $q$-difference operator $\widehat A (\widehat x, \widehat y; q)$ annihilates the partition function of Chern-Simons theory / matrix model / B-model / instanton partition function is easy to refine. Just like each of these partition functions becomes $t$-dependent, so does the operator $\widehat A (\widehat x, \widehat y; q,t)$ that annihilates it. blocks.title: The gamma factors for symmetric and anti-symmetric representations
From partition functions to superpolynomials
blocks.content:
As we already explained around [\[superPdef\]](#superPdef){reference-type="eqref" reference="superPdef"}, the reduced colored superpolynomial ${\cal P}^R (K; a,q,t)$ is defined as the Poincaré polynomial of the triply graded homology ${\cal H }^R_{i,j,k} (K)$ that categorifies the colored HOMFLY polynomial $P^R (K;a,q)$. Here, the word "reduced" means that the normalization is such that $P^R ({\,\raisebox{-.08cm}{\includegraphics[width=.37cm]{unknot}}\,}) = 1$. Although normalization is one of the delicate points one has to worry about, luckily it will not be a major issue for us here.

blocks.title: Homological algebra of colored knot invariants
Recursion relations for homological knot invariants
blocks.content:
In this section we ﬁnd recursion relations which are satisﬁed by homological knot invariants,
therefore, providing concrete examples for one of the new volume conjectures proposed in
section 2.
In other words, we ﬁnd reﬁned quantum A-polynomials bAref(bx, by; q, t). These are the
objects which generalize the unreﬁned quantum curves considered e.g. in [3, 17, 59, 7, 19].

blocks.content: We can now analyze under what conditions the refined $A$-polynomials which we found earlier are quantizable. Since we already found the explicit form of such refined polynomials $A^{\textrm{ref}}(x,y;t)$, in order to test quantizability we can simply apply the condition ([\[tempered\]](#tempered){reference-type="ref" reference="tempered"}). To this end, we need to identify face polynomials associated to the Newton polygons of various knots discussed earlier. blocks.title: Examples coming from refined BPS invariants
blocks.content:
[]{#sec:Bmodel label="sec:Bmodel"}

It is known that $\mathcal{N}=2$ gauge theories can be geometrically engineered by considering type II string theory on appropriate toric Calabi-Yau manifolds [@engineering]. The corresponding mirror manifolds have the form of a hypersurface $$z_1 z_2 \; = \; A(x,y)    \label{Amirror}$$ in ${\mathbb C}^2 \times {\mathbb C}^{*\, 2}$. Upon the suitable identification of parameters the mirror curve $A(x,y)=0$ agrees with the Seiberg-Witten curve of the 5-dimensional theory on a circle, and its appropriate scaling limit reproduces the ordinary Seiberg-Witten cur

blocks.content: In this section we derive the refined quantum curves relevant in the context of the open BPS state counting (or topological string theory). They can be regarded as refined and quantum versions of mirror curves $A(x,y)=0$ which appear in the mirror geometry ([\[Amirror\]](#Amirror){reference-type="ref" reference="Amirror"}) for toric three-folds. Specifically, we consider open refined topological string amplitudes for branes along preferred directions, in general framing, for ${\mathbb C}^3$ and conifold geometries. blocks.content: We now repeat the above calculation for the conifold, whose ordinary mirror curve in general framing takes the form [@abmodel]: $$A^{\text{ref}} (x,y;q_1=1) = 1 - y + x(-y)^f + Q x (-y)^{f+1} \; = \; 0 \,.    \label{mirrorConif}$$ To find the refined and quantum version of this curve, we again consider the brane located along the preferred direction of the conifold. More precisely, we wish to consider the brane amplitude normalized by the closed string partition function. blocks.content: Once we found the refined quantum curves, we can easily determine the classical refined mirror curves. Namely, much as in the knot theory examples, we can find them in two ways.
